title: Device Fingerprinting Security Checklist - Protect Your Privacy
metaDescription: Complete checklist to protect against device fingerprinting. Stop invisible tracking that persists after clearing cookies with these proven methods.
intro: Device fingerprinting allows websites to track you even after clearing cookies by collecting unique information about your browser and device. This checklist provides actionable steps to protect against these invisible tracking techniques.

items.task: Use a browser that handles WebGL for you
items.why: WebGL reads how your graphics hardware draws, which is stable across sessions and tied to the machine. Browsers that randomise or block that output are what break the link.
items.howTo: Turning WebGL off outright makes you rarer, not commoner. Prefer a browser that randomises or standardises the output: Brave does it by default, Firefox does it under privacy.resistFingerprinting, and Tor Browser and Mullvad Browser ship it on.

items.task: Block or spoof HTML5 Canvas fingerprinting
items.why: Canvas fingerprinting forces your browser to draw hidden images, creating unique signatures based on your system's rendering differences.
items.howTo: In Firefox, install the CanvasBlocker extension or set privacy.resistFingerprinting to true in about:config. Brave, Tor Browser and Mullvad Browser protect canvas readings by default.

items.task: Disable WebRTC to prevent IP leaks
items.why: WebRTC can expose your real IP address even when using VPN and provides additional fingerprinting data points.
items.howTo: Firefox: Set media.peerconnection.enabled to false in about:config. Chrome: Install the WebRTC Leak Prevent extension. Brave: Set 'WebRTC IP handling policy' to 'Disable non-proxied UDP' in Settings > Privacy and security.

items.why: A switcher extension makes you rarer, not commoner: the faked string rarely matches what the rest of your browser reports, and that mismatch is itself distinctive.
items.howTo: Don't install a User-Agent Switcher. Keep the browser up to date so your string matches everyone else on the current version, and if you want real fingerprint resistance use Tor Browser or Firefox's resistFingerprinting.

items.task: Cut down the extensions you run
items.why: Plugins are gone: no current browser runs Flash, Java or Silverlight, and there is no plugins section left in settings. Extensions are what remains, and an unusual set of them is fingerprintable.
items.howTo: Open the extensions page and remove anything you don't use weekly. Extensions that inject content into pages are the most detectable, so keep the list short and ordinary.

items.why: Your timezone is easily accessible to websites and combined with other data points creates a more unique fingerprint profile.
items.howTo: Firefox with privacy.resistFingerprinting, Tor Browser and Mullvad Browser report the same UTC time zone to every site. In other browsers, a time-zone spoofing extension can do the same.

items.why: Audio fingerprinting analyzes how your system processes audio signals, creating unique identifiers based on hardware differences.
items.howTo: Install AudioContext Fingerprint Defender extension or use browsers with built-in audio protection like Tor Browser.

items.why: Websites can detect installed fonts on your system, creating unique combinations that identify your device across different sites.
items.howTo: Turn on privacy.resistFingerprinting in Firefox, which limits the fonts sites can detect to a standard set, or use Tor Browser or Mullvad Browser, which ship a fixed font list. Blocking known fingerprinting scripts with uBlock Origin also helps.

items.why: Unique screen resolutions, especially on mobile devices or multi-monitor setups, create easily identifiable fingerprint signatures.
items.howTo: Use Resolution Changer extension to report common resolutions like 1920x1080, or browse in full-screen mode to limit resolution detection.

items.why: CPU cores, memory, graphics cards, and other hardware specs create highly unique fingerprints that are difficult to change.
items.howTo: Use browsers that limit hardware API access like Tor Browser, or enable strict privacy settings in Firefox about:config for hardware queries.

items.why: Battery level and charging status provide additional unique identifiers, especially on mobile devices with varying battery health.
items.howTo: Firefox and Safari don't give websites battery information, so there's nothing to change there. In Chrome and Edge, block the Battery Status API with an extension, or use Firefox for sensitive browsing.

items.why: Regular testing helps you understand how unique your browser appears and whether your protection measures are working effectively.
items.howTo: Visit AmIUnique.org, coveryourtracks.eff.org (the EFF's renamed Panopticlick) and BrowserLeaks.com monthly to test your fingerprint. Note what changes after each protection you add.

items.task: Use different browsers for different activities
items.why: Compartmentalizing your browsing creates separate fingerprint profiles, making it harder to track your activities across different contexts.
items.howTo: Use Tor Browser or Mullvad Browser for sensitive browsing, Firefox with extensions for daily use, and a stock browser for sites that break with modifications.

items.why: Many fingerprinting attempts happen invisibly. Detection tools help you identify which sites are attempting to fingerprint your device.
items.howTo: Install Privacy Badger or Ghostery, which both show what they blocked on a page. uBlock Origin's logger gives the fullest view but exists only on Firefox; uBlock Origin Lite on Chrome has no logger.

items.task: Rotate browser profiles and clear data
items.why: Fingerprint protection doesn't clear stored identifiers: cookies, local storage and cache entries can still link your visits over time. A fresh profile removes them.
items.howTo: Create new Firefox profiles monthly, or set your browser to delete cookies and site data when you close it. Clear all browser data, including local storage and IndexedDB.

items.why: VPNs hide your IP but don't prevent fingerprinting. Combining both provides comprehensive protection against tracking techniques.
items.howTo: Use a no-logs VPN service with your fingerprint protection setup. Ensure WebRTC is disabled to prevent IP leaks that could correlate with fingerprints.

pro_tips: Tor Browser and Mullvad Browser come with fingerprinting protection already set up, including canvas protection, letterboxing and a UTC time zone. Brave randomizes canvas, WebGL and audio readings by default.
Don't make your browser too unique - overly aggressive fingerprint protection can actually make you more identifiable. Aim to blend in with common configurations.
Test your fingerprint protection on multiple testing sites, as each site checks different fingerprinting vectors and may reveal weaknesses in your setup.

Mobile browsers are particularly vulnerable to fingerprinting due to sensor access and touch capabilities. On Android, Tor Browser and Brave both protect against fingerprinting; on iPhone, Safari's Private Browsing turns on Apple's advanced fingerprinting protection.
Fingerprinting protection often breaks some websites. Keep a separate browser profile with standard settings for sites that require full functionality.
